interactions.summary: Jiang answers his own purgatory question by insisting that the suffering is self-imposed penance chosen by free will rather than an externally forced punishment.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student prompt followed by Jiang correction and lecture expansion.

interactions.summary: The reading moves from Statius's explanation of the quake into his self-identification, the dating of Titus's vengeance, and his extravagant reverence for Virgil.

Jiang glosses the dating around Titus, then frames Statius as willing to extend purgatorial suffering for a chance to meet Virgil and uses that excess to argue that Virgil feels summoned rather than invented.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang explanation with noisy ASR around the quote.

speaker_notes.note: This segment is heavily corrupted by ASR, but the surrounding Jiang gloss makes clear that Statius is declaring his admiration for Virgil and willingness to prolong penance for a chance to meet him.

claims.claim: Jiang says purgatorial suffering is not God inflicting punishment on souls but souls freely choosing penance to make themselves worthy of God.
Jiang explicitly calls this complete free will: no one makes the souls do these punishments, because they themselves want the suffering that purifies them before meeting God.
Jiang uses the prom analogy to say penance is like deliberately presenting your best self before an awaited meeting rather than merely serving a sentence.
Jiang dates Titus's vengeance to the year 70 and says Christians read the destruction of the second temple as vengeance for the crucifixion.
Jiang interprets Statius as valuing one encounter with Virgil so highly that he would accept another year of purgatorial suffering for it.
Jiang says Virgil feels less like a literary fabrication than a summoned presence because Dante's portrayal captures such specific, excessive human realism.

signature_moments.moment: Purgatory is redefined as souls punishing themselves because they want to be worthy of God.
signature_moments.source_phrase: It's not God punishing us. It's we're punishing ourselves
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's sharpest free-will formulation for why purgatorial suffering exists at all.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns penance into the desire to show up at the divine meeting in your best form, like dressing for prom.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's like going to the prom
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The analogy domesticates an abstract theological point without softening its voluntary rigor.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil is said to be too real to have been merely invented and instead must be summoned.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's no way Dante could have created Virgil
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This condenses Jiang's larger claim that the poem is tapping a reality deeper than authorial fabrication.

chronology_notes.note: This packet is a strong June 26 statement of Jiang's view that purgation is chosen self-purification and that Dante's figures can feel summoned rather than merely authored.

uncertainty_notes.note: These spans contain significant ASR corruption, so the semantic pass relies on the clearer adjacent Jiang gloss for Statius's timeline and Virgil-devotion framing.
